title.en: Creation day and Hashem's first plan

summary.en: On Chaf-Hei Adar the Mashgiach recalls the Gemara's dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nisan, and explains that when the Torah speaks of Hashem 'regretting', it speaks in our terms, since even Adam's sin was in His plan. He describes the world Hashem intended with Adam HaRishon on Rosh Chodesh Nisan: a Gan Eden without death, spoiled by the sin of the Eitz HaDaas.

title.en: Avraham Avinu, the spring neshama

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every person has his time, and Avraham Avinu's time is Nisan, the spring. He paints spring as a revival from the shrouds of winter, brings Shir Hashirim's call to wake up, and lists the events of Avraham's life that took place on Pesach.

title.en: The second and third Nisan

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Hashem's second attempt, localized to one nation descended from Avraham and brought out of Mitzrayim in Nisan, which the Egel spoiled. The third attempt, localized to the Mishkan, was spoiled by Nadav and Avihu, and Rashi on 'Mishkan haEidus' hints that the two Batei Mikdash would be destroyed.

title.en: The fourth Nisan and never despairing

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the promised fourth Nisan with the third Beis HaMikdash, when death will end, as the Rambam describes at the end of Hilchos Melachim. He connects this to the Haftarah of the dry bones read on Pesach, and draws from the Mishkan built and taken apart for seven days that a person who falls must get up and try again.

title.en: Nisan, the month of chesed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nisan is a month of chesed because it is Avraham Avinu's month, and that creation in Nisan reflects building the world with chesed rather than din. Jews always raise chesed over din: washing the right hand first, putting on the right shoe first but tying the left, binding tefillin on the left, and writing from the right.

title.en: Harnessed chesed: moon, sun and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts Esav, who writes from the left and follows the sun of din, with Yishmael, the refuse of Avraham's chesed, whose unbridled chesed turns to immorality. Jews count by the moon of chesed but harness it to the solar year through the leap year, while the Arabs' months drift through the seasons; likewise Shabbos stands in the middle between Friday and Sunday.

title.en: Matzah, the key that opens

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nisan goes straight, like the aleph-beis, and opens with chesed: maos chittim and 'whoever is hungry, come and eat'. Matzah, which Targum calls 'patira', is the key that opens the doors of chesed; on Pesach night the storehouses of tal open, as the Targum Yonasan says about Yitzchak's brachos, and tal in gematria joins the Name of Hashem and brings down the tal of techiyas hameisim.

title.en: Matzah, Mah and the night of questions

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Pesach comes from a world beyond understanding, the world of 'Mah', and that matzah equals three times Mah (45) while bread equals three times the Name Havaya (26). That is why the Haggadah begins with questions, and why Pesach is renewal, when people buy new clothing and take out vessels unused for a year.

title.en: Matzah above time and space

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that this world is bound by time and space, as shown by how witnesses are examined on when and where, while bread needs both to rise. Matzah is given no time and takes no space, because it belongs to a higher world, and on Pesach a Jew is to rise above them. He ends with the two pieces of matzah at the Seder, the Afikoman pointing to the future redemption.

title.en: Pesach as the beginning and the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that although Shavuos and Sukkos are higher, Pesach is the beginning, when a Jew ties himself to Hashem, so chametz carries kares, the opposite of that bond, and an arel may not eat the korban Pesach. He brings the Radbaz's question why chametz is treated more strictly than any other aveirah.

title.en: The tzaddik's kernel of wheat

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard from the Klausenberger Rebbe about a tzaddik who prepared a perfectly chametz-free Pesach and found a kernel of wheat in his soup. Through a she'eilas chalom he learned that he had not davened for a kosher Pesach, and that a bird had dropped the kernel through the chimney. The Mashgiach closes with a brachah for a kosher Pesach in Yerushalayim.

catalogTitle: א - ביאור המדרש על הפס' “קראתי למאהבי המה רמוני'” זמן לעבוד ה' באבילות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Midrash that the prophets 'deceived' Klal Yisrael to keep their hope for Moshiach alive, and teaches that in the days of mourning the way to Yerushalayim and to Heaven is through tears, broken hearts and the prayer Moshe Rabbeinu left unfinished.

abstract.en: Drawing on the Yaaros Devash, the Mashgiach brings the Midrash on 'I called to my lovers, they deceived me': the prophets instituted terumah and maaser outside Eretz Yisrael so that Jews would believe Moshiach is near. Since the end was hidden lest Jews despair, this 'deception' kept hope alive, and that hope after two thousand years is itself a sign of redemption. He explains Yerushalayim as yirah and shalom, the place of the Shechinah to which every Jewish soul is drawn, and says that in these days the passport to Heaven is weeping, not joy. Through a question of the Avnei Nezer on R' Yochanan he shows that Hashem Himself burned the Beis HaMikdash, renewed each moment, and that warm tefillos and tears will rebuild it. He ends with Vaeschanan: Moshe's prayers lacked one more, which Klal Yisrael must complete on Tisha B'Av.

en: The Mashgiach brings that the end of the exile was hidden so that Jews would not fall into despair over how long it would take.
Every Jew's soul comes from the Kisei HaKavod and is naturally drawn to Yerushalayim, so in the time of churban he naturally feels its absence.
Hashem fills a lack according to how much it is felt, so the more Klal Yisrael feels the absence of Yerushalayim, the more it hastens its rebuilding.
Tisha B'Av is the 'end of days' of the year, its lowest point, when a pure heart can hear the Shechinah weeping over Yerushalayim.
Yerushalayim is being built now, year after year, from stones made of broken Jewish hearts and tears.
Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach says every year without the Beis HaMikdash is a new churban, as the world sinks lower and foreign influences break through the walls.
Every Tisha B'Av is a new battle for Yerushalayim, and every Jew must be a soldier whose weapons are the kinos, the weeping and the mourning.

title.en: The Midrash: 'they deceived me'

summary.en: The Mashgiach draws on the Yaaros Devash, which brings the Midrash that the 'lovers' who 'deceived' Klal Yisrael are the prophets who instituted terumah and maaser outside Eretz Yisrael. He asks what deception this was, and brings that the end of the exile was hidden so that Jews would not despair over its length.

title.en: Why the prophets kept hope alive

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a takanah meant to last two thousand years would make little sense; the prophets made it so Jews would feel Moshiach is near. He speaks of the many disappointed hopes over the kitzim and says that the Jews' hope after two thousand years is itself a sign they must be redeemed.

title.en: What Yerushalayim is

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Yerushalayim as the city of G-dliness, a piece of heaven on earth and the place where the Shechinah rests, made of yirah and shalom like Shabbos. Every Jew whose soul comes from the Kisei HaKavod is drawn to it, like the strings of Dovid HaMelech's harp.

title.en: Feeling the lack of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that mourning in these days is the natural feeling of a Jew that Yerushalayim is missing, and that Hashem fills a lack as much as it is felt. He brings the Chasam Sofer on the Yerushalmi about the earlier and later generations, explaining with the parable of a man who knows his heart is weak and does nothing.

title.en: Weeping: the passport to Heaven now

summary.en: Usually simcha is the passport to Heaven, since 'strength and joy are in His place'. But in these days Hashem has called for weeping and mourning, the angels cry and the King of the Midrash puts out the lamps, so the Mashgiach says one reaches Heaven now only through weeping, sharing the Shechinah's sorrow.

title.en: End of days; building with broken hearts

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Chasam Sofer that 'the end of days' in Devarim is Tisha B'Av, the lowest point of the year, when a cleansed heart can hear the Shechinah weeping. Jews must not be silent, and 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem' means Yerushalayim is being built now from broken hearts, which Hashem will heal into joy.

title.en: R' Yitzchak Nafcha pleases both students

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara where R' Ami and R' Assi sat before R' Yitzchak Nafcha, one wanting halachah and the other agadah. He told them a teaching on fire, 'I lit a fire in Zion', together with the halachah of damage by fire, and the Mashgiach asks how this satisfied both.

title.en: The Avnei Nezer's question on R' Yochanan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Avnei Nezer: R' Yochanan said he would have fixed the fast on the tenth of Av, when most of the burning happened, yet he also holds 'isho mishum chitzav', which by the Nimukei Yosef attributes a fire to its start. He begins his answer with two modes of Divine conduct, knowledge and free choice, and why a murderer cannot plead that Hashem runs the world.

title.en: Hashem burned it, moment by moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the Beis HaMikdash was above time and place, so Hashem, not Titus, burned it; and since Hashem creates everything anew each moment (Nefesh HaChaim), each moment of the burning was a new fire, which fits R' Yochanan and reconciles the agadah and the halachah for his students R' Ami and R' Assi. The fire that burned Zion was the sins; the fire that will rebuild it is the warmth of Jewish tefillos and tears.

title.en: Vaeschanan: praying in a time of distress

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that Tisha B'Av always comes with parshas Vaeschanan, and each reading awakens its time. He explains that one cannot always daven, and brings the Yalkut that Moshe's prayer teaches all generations to pray in distress; his distress was that he could not enter Eretz Yisrael and see Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: A new churban each year; Tisha B'Av as battle

summary.en: Citing the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach says each year is a new churban, describing how the culture of the street, Hollywood and the universities breaks into the beis medrash. Tisha B'Av, like crying out in time of war, is a battle in which every Jew must be a soldier, fighting with kinos and mourning.

title.en: Moshe's one missing prayer

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why this was Moshe's worst distress, and answers that like R' Chanina ben Dosa he could sense his prayer was not accepted, yet pushed to break through. His 515 prayers were in truth accepted but lacked one more, which Klal Yisrael must complete through the generations, especially when Tisha B'Av meets Vaeschanan, since we are now in history's 'end of days'.
